0.title: The Letter of Jude: Contend for the Faith
0.overview:
Jude is one of the most neglected letters in the New Testament. Most Christians know the doxology at the end — and it is magnificent — but could not tell you what comes before it. What comes before it is some of the most urgent, vivid, and pastorally charged writing in the entire canon. Jude is a fire-bell.

The author identifies himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). He does not say “brother of the Lord” — though he almost certainly was. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name “Judas” among the brothers of Jesus, and James was the recognized head of the Jerusalem church. Jude had credentials that would have opened every door in the early Christian world: raised in the same household as the Son of God, converted after the resurrection, brother to the most respected Jewish-Christian leader of the first generation. He uses none of it. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. The biological relationship, once the most important fact about him, has been swallowed up by a greater reality: the resurrection has changed the category. He no longer has a brother who happens to be the Messiah; he has a Lord who happens to have been his brother.

The occasion for the letter is stated plainly in v. 3. Jude had intended to write about “our common salvation” — a warm, constructive letter celebrating the faith they shared. He never wrote it. The crisis was too pressing. False teachers had “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4), and Jude found himself writing an alarm instead of a celebration. The letter we have is not the letter he planned. This matters pastorally: faithful ministry sometimes means setting aside what we intended to say in order to say what the moment requires.

How is Jude related to 2 Peter 2, which says many of the same things? Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude; some think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on common teaching. The more likely reading is that Peter knew Jude’s letter and adapted it. That takes nothing from either: an inspired writer may use another’s words, as the prophets and apostles often did.

The letter is twenty-five verses. It has no chapter breaks. It is a single sustained argument that moves from the alarm (vv. 3–4), through the evidence (vv. 5–16), to the counter-strategy for the faithful (vv. 17–23), and finally to one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture (vv. 24–25). The fire and the doxology belong together. The letter that begins with danger ends with adoration — and the adoration is not escapism. It is the theological ground on which the whole letter stands. You can contend for the faith without bitterness, rescue others without losing yourself, hold on under pressure — because the One who keeps you is infinitely more powerful than everything that threatens you.

1.title: Contend, Hold Fast, Adore
1.overview:
Jude’s one chapter moves in four steps. He states why he writes: contend for the faith, because false teachers have slipped in (vv. 3–4). He gives the evidence: three examples of judgment on people who had privilege and despised it (vv. 5–7), then a vivid portrait of the false teachers who are repeating the pattern (vv. 8–16). He turns to the faithful: remember, build up, pray, keep yourselves in God’s love and rescue the wavering (vv. 17–23). And he ends with God, who is able to keep his people from stumbling (vv. 24–25).

The order matters. The darkness of vv. 5–16 is framed by the people who are “called, beloved… and kept” (v. 1) and the God “who is able to keep you” (v. 24). Jude warns in order to make his readers brave, not anxious: the courage of people who know they are held.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called (God summoned them), beloved in God the Father (they rest in his love now) and kept for Jesus Christ (guarded until he comes). Every alarm that follows is heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called, Beloved, Kept

Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called, beloved in God the Father, kept for Jesus Christ. The warnings are heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church shaken by false teachers is first reminded of its security.

Now: A believer who fears drifting away begins where Jude begins: not with their grip on God, but with his grip on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.

Meaning first. Jude is a short, urgent letter calling believers to contend for the faith against ungodly intruders. Jude greets those who are called, loved by God and kept for Jesus Christ (vv. 1–2). He had intended to write about their shared salvation, but had to urge them instead to fight for the faith delivered once for all to the saints, because ungodly people had slipped in who turn God’s grace into a licence for immorality and deny Jesus Christ (vv. 3–4). He reminds them of God’s past judgements: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who abandoned their position, and Sodom and Gomorrah (vv. 5–7). The intruders defile the flesh, reject authority and slander heavenly beings, where even the archangel Michael left judgement to the Lord; they follow Cain, Balaam and Korah, and are like hidden reefs, waterless clouds, dead trees, wild waves and wandering stars (vv. 8–13). Enoch prophesied their judgement when the Lord comes with his holy ones; they are grumblers, boasters and flatterers (vv. 14–16). The apostles foretold such scoffers, who divide and are devoid of the Spirit (vv. 17–19). But believers must build themselves up in the faith, pray in the Spirit, keep themselves in God’s love, wait for Christ’s mercy, and show mercy to the doubting and the endangered (vv. 20–23). The letter ends with one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and present you blameless before his glory with great joy be glory forever (vv. 24–25). The whole alarm is framed by two words about God: at the start, his people are kept; at the end, he is able to keep them.

The setting. Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5) but came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). He is named among Jesus’ brothers in Mark 6:3. The date is uncertain, perhaps AD 60–80. His readers are unknown, probably Jewish Christians, given his use of Old Testament and Jewish examples. Much of the letter closely parallels 2 Peter 2. Imagine what it meant for this man to write at all. He grew up in the same house as Jesus in Nazareth, shared meals and work with him, and thought him out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Now he writes of Jesus Christ as our only Master and Lord.

Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ. “Servant” (doulos) is slave: one whose will belongs to another. Like James (James 1:1), Jude does not call himself Jesus’ brother, but his slave. He could have written brother of the Lord and silenced every critic in the room. He had a credential that only he and James among the New Testament writers possessed, and he chose not to use it. This is not false modesty; it is theology. The resurrection changed everything. Before Easter, Jude had a brother who was becoming increasingly difficult to explain. After Easter, he had a Lord. The most intimate human relationship in his life was now secondary to the relationship of faith. When Jude calls himself a slave of Jesus, he is confessing that Easter happened and that it reordered everything. The relationship that matters is not physical family but faith (Mark 3:35).

And brother of James. James was the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church, a pillar (Galatians 2:9). Jude appeals to him not to claim status but to establish identity. The readers would have known James and would have trusted any letter from his household. That is the credential Jude does use: not his physical closeness to Jesus but his connection to the leader the community already knew and trusted. Identifying himself through James gives his letter weight.

To those who are called. Then three descriptions, each doing theological work. “Called” (klētois) is God’s effectual call (Romans 8:28–30): the divine summons that brought them to faith. It is God’s act, not their initiative.

Beloved in God the Father. “Beloved” (ēgapēmenois) is perfect tense: having been loved and remaining loved. God’s love, set on them in eternity, continues. And they are loved in him: held within the sphere of his love, which is the only love that is unchanging and permanent. Before Jude says a word about danger, he tells them where they live.

And kept for Jesus Christ. “Kept” (tetērēmenois) is perfect tense again: guarded and still guarded. Kept by God for Christ, until his return, as a treasure is kept for its owner, or a bride for her bridegroom. They are not maintaining themselves; they are being maintained. Three great truths frame the letter: called, loved, kept. And it ends with the God who is able to keep (v. 24). Amid all the warnings, believers are secure. The people being warned are divinely held.

If I am kept, why does this letter warn me so strongly? Because warnings are one of the ways God keeps his people. A father who holds his child’s hand on a cliff path also says, stay away from the edge. The warning does not mean he might let go; it is part of how he holds. Jude will tell you to keep yourselves in the love of God (v. 21), and then end by praising the God who keeps you (v. 24). Read every warning in this letter as the voice of the One who is guarding you, not as a sign that he might fail.

May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you. “Multiplied” (plēthyntheiē) is increased, abundant. The greeting is distinctive, slightly different from Paul’s usual grace and peace. In a letter about the danger of false teaching and the urgency of contending, Jude opens with what God gives his people: mercy that does not hold their failures against them, peace with God that holds the heart steady, and love that holds them no matter what. And he prays that each will be multiplied, because those who must contend need more of all three, not less.

What it does not mean. Kept does not mean believers are passive. Jude will command them to keep themselves (v. 21). God keeps them, and they keep themselves, both together.

In a sentence. From Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, to those who have been called, who are loved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: mercy, peace and love be yours in abundance.

On a Tuesday. Before you face anything hard today, a difficult conversation, a temptation, a worrying piece of news, say these three words to yourself: called, loved, kept. They are true of every believer, and they are true in the past tense and the present together. And if someone in your family does not yet believe, remember Jude: the brothers who thought Jesus mad became his servants. Keep praying.

For worship. The God who called us did not call us and then leave us at the door. He loved us before we existed, and he has not stopped. He is keeping us now, guarding us like a treasure for the day his Son comes to claim his own. Jude grew up with Jesus and did not believe; then he saw him risen, and bowed. The brother became a servant, and the servant found that his Master had been keeping him all along. Mercy, peace and love are not rations from a reluctant God. They are multiplied, poured out by the Father, through the Son, upon people who are his.
verseByVerse.note: Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, came to faith after the resurrection. Much of his letter is closely paralleled in 2 Peter 2.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude meant to write a warm letter about “our common salvation”, but the danger forced him to write an alarm instead. The result is one of the key sentences in the New Testament on how the church relates to its doctrine: “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.” The faith is given, complete, and must be guarded.
verseByVerse.theology:
Contend for the Faith

The faith was delivered once for all to the saints. False teachers turn grace into sensuality and deny the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jude set aside the letter he wanted to write because the danger was urgent.

Now: Contend as someone who loves the people being misled, not as someone who enjoys a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation. “Very eager” (pasan spoudēn poioumenos) is making every effort. “Common salvation” (koinēs sōtērias) is shared salvation: the salvation all believers have in common, Jew and Gentile, slave and free. Jude had planned a positive letter about it. The intended letter was never written. A celebratory letter about the faith they all shared gave way to something harder and more urgent. We learn something about Jude’s character from the letter he wanted to write and could not. He is not a controversialist who enjoys a fight; he is a pastor who would have preferred to celebrate but found the situation demanded something else. It is the people who love the gospel most who find it hardest to watch it being distorted.

I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith. “Necessary” (anankē) is compulsion: circumstances forced a change of plan. “Contend” (epagōnizesthai) is to fight earnestly, to struggle hard, as an athlete strains in a contest; from it comes our word agony. “The faith” (tē pistei) is not personal trust here, but the body of truth believed, the gospel.

That was once for all delivered to the saints. “Once for all” (hapax) is a single, final, complete delivery. “Delivered” (paradotheisē) is handed down, entrusted as a tradition, like a precious deposit placed in someone’s keeping. The faith was given by God through the apostles, complete and unchangeable. Nothing can be added to it or subtracted from it. This is the basis of the closed canon and sola Scriptura: the apostolic faith, recorded in Scripture, is final. And it was delivered to the saints: not to an elite, not to a priesthood, but to all God’s holy people. Every believer is a trustee of it.

What is the faith that was once for all delivered? The body of apostolic teaching about Christ, given complete and not to be added to: who he is, God and man; what he did, in his life, death for sinners, resurrection and ascension; what he will do, in his return and judgement; and how sinners are saved, by grace through faith, and called to holy lives. That is why the church has no new revelation to wait for; it has a faith to keep. And contending for it means teaching it clearly, holding it fast, exposing error and rescuing those caught by it (vv. 22–23), with the gentleness of a servant of the Lord (2 Timothy 2:24–25), not the bitterness of a quarreller.

For certain people have crept in unnoticed. “Crept in unnoticed” (pareisedysan) is slipped in sideways, sneaked in, like spies infiltrating a camp, or someone entering by a side door. They were not announced; they did not come in openly. They were inside the church. They came the way dangerous teaching almost always comes: gradually, plausibly, using the church’s own language. The most dangerous false teaching is not the kind that is obviously alien; it is the kind that sounds like the gospel while quietly removing its foundations.

Who long ago were designated for this condemnation. “Long ago” (palai). “Designated” (progegrammenoi) is written beforehand, marked out in advance. Either their condemnation was written beforehand in Scripture, in the examples that follow, or God had appointed it in advance. Their judgement is not a surprise to God. God’s condemnation of the ungodly is not a reactive improvisation; the judgement of those who pervert his grace was written into the pattern of history long before they appeared.

Does long ago were designated for this condemnation mean that God predestined these people to be condemned? Some read it as God’s decree; others as the condemnation long foretold in Scripture for people like them, which Jude goes on to show with Israel, the angels, Sodom and Enoch’s prophecy. The word itself most naturally means written beforehand, and Jude’s following examples suggest that the condemnation of such people was written in Scripture long ago. Behind that writing stands God’s sovereign governance of all things, so that nothing about these men takes him by surprise. But their sin is their own: they perverted grace into sensuality, and they are justly judged for what they freely chose.

Ungodly people. “Ungodly” (asebeis) is irreverent, without regard for God. It is a key word of Jude (vv. 4, 15, 18). They may be religious, but God is not feared in their lives.

Who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality. “Pervert” (metatithentes) is to change, alter, transpose, turn into something else. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is unrestrained immorality. They twisted grace into a licence to sin: since we are forgiven, sin does not matter (Romans 6:1–2). This is antinomianism. They took grace, the most beautiful and transforming reality in the universe, and turned it into a moral blank cheque. This is not merely an ethical failure; it is a theological one. A grace that permits anything is not the grace of the New Testament, which trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions (Titus 2:12). Any theology that produces licentiousness rather than holiness has not understood grace; it has replaced it with something that wears grace’s clothing.

And deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. “Master” (despotēs) is sovereign, and “Lord” (kyrios). Grammatically, only Master and Lord both refer to Jesus Christ, a strong statement of his deity. They denied his lordship by their lives and perhaps by their teaching (2 Peter 2:1; Titus 1:16). To claim his name while living as though his lordship makes no claim on the body is to deny him in practice. Jude’s two charges are not separate: the perversion of grace and the denial of the Lord are two aspects of a single failure. A Christ who does not reign over the moral life is not the Christ of the New Testament.

Where Christians differ: is the faith still developing through new revelation? Some churches hold that doctrine develops through ongoing revelation or the church’s teaching office, adding new dogmas over time; some charismatics expect new prophetic revelation. Verdict: Jude says the faith was delivered once for all. The apostolic deposit is complete. The church’s understanding of Scripture may deepen, but no new doctrine may be added. Scripture alone is the final rule of faith, and the canon is closed.

Does stressing grace not lead people to take sin lightly? Real grace never does. The grace that forgives also transforms: it unites us to Christ, gives us a new heart, and teaches us to say no to ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). Those who use grace as an excuse show that they have not received it. The answer to antinomianism is not less grace, as if the gospel needed to be balanced with a little law to keep people in line, but a true understanding of grace. People who have truly been forgiven much love much, and love keeps God’s commandments (John 14:15).

How do I contend without becoming a contentious person? Contend for the faith, not for your preferences, and contend about what matters most: the person and work of Christ, the gospel of grace, the holiness it produces. Know your Bible well enough to do it. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), gently, without mockery, seeking to win people rather than to defeat them. Distinguish between those who teach error and those who have been confused by it (vv. 22–23). And pray for those you disagree with. A contender who does not pray for his opponents has become a quarreller.

What it does not mean. Contend does not mean being quarrelsome or harsh. It means standing firm for the truth, earnestly and lovingly (v. 22; 2 Timothy 2:24–25).

In a sentence. Dear friends, although I was very eager to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt compelled to write and urge you to contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to God’s holy people. For certain individuals whose condemnation was written about long ago have secretly slipped in among you. They are ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into a licence for immorality and deny Jesus Christ, our only Sovereign and Lord.

On a Tuesday. Learn the faith well enough to contend for it. Is there a teaching that turns grace into permission to sin? Stand against it. Take one central truth this week, the deity of Christ, justification by faith, the return of Christ, and learn to explain it simply with two or three Bible passages. And ask honestly whether there is any area of your own life where you are quietly using grace as an excuse.

For worship. The faith was delivered once for all, because the Saviour did his work once for all. He lived the perfect life, died the one death that atones, rose and reigns, and nothing needs to be added. The grace of our God is not a licence but a liberation, which breaks the chains of sin and teaches the freed to walk in holiness. And over this grace stands our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ, who bought his people and will not let them be stolen by those who creep in. We have a common salvation, shared by every saint, and a faith worth contending for, because it is the truth about him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three examples make one point: privilege does not protect from judgment. Israel was redeemed from Egypt; the angels stood in God’s presence; Sodom had righteous Lot in its midst. Each had unusual exposure to God, each turned from him, and each was judged. The false teachers are repeating the pattern.
verseByVerse.theology:
Privilege Is No Shield

Israel redeemed from Egypt, angels who left their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah all show that privilege does not exempt anyone from judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers belonged to the church but were walking Israel’s, the angels’ and Sodom’s road.

Now: The person most at risk is not the one who has never heard, but the one who has heard so often that the gospel has become background noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.

Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it. “Once” (hapax) is once for all, the same word as in verse 3. They knew these truths; they needed reminding (2 Peter 1:12). Jude, like Peter, believes that the church’s great need is not novelty but memory.

That Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt. Some manuscripts read the Lord, others Jesus, others God. Jesus has strong early support and is probably original, as the harder reading: scribes were more likely to smooth it to the Lord than to introduce Jesus into an Old Testament scene. If so, Jude attributes the exodus to the pre-existent Christ, as Paul does when he says that the rock that followed Israel was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). A striking statement of Christ’s eternal deity. The same Jesus who would later become flesh was the divine agent of the exodus. And in either reading the theological point is the same: the God who redeemed Israel afterward destroyed those who did not believe. Salvation and judgement belong to the same Lord.

Afterward destroyed those who did not believe. “Afterward” (to deuteron) is literally the second time. Numbers 14 records the pivotal moment: Israel heard the report of the twelve spies, believed the ten who said they could not take the land, and so refused to trust the God who had brought them out of Egypt with signs and wonders. The entire generation over twenty years old died in the wilderness (Numbers 14; Hebrews 3:16–19). The same people whom God redeemed from Egypt perished for unbelief. Being part of God’s people outwardly does not guarantee salvation. No historical privilege, no exodus, no baptism, no church membership, substitutes for persevering faith.

Does this mean that the saved can perish? Israel as a nation was brought out of Egypt, but the generation who did not believe died in the wilderness. Outward deliverance and membership among God’s people are not the same as saving faith. Some read the example as a warning that true believers may be lost; the more likely reading is that it warns professing believers not to trust in privileges without faith.

And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority. The second example. “Position of authority” (archē) is rule, domain, rank. Angels who abandoned their God-given place. These were among the highest of created beings, beings of glory and power who stood before the throne of God, and they left their assigned place. Jewish tradition (1 Enoch) connected this with the sons of God and the daughters of men (Genesis 6:1–4), as in 2 Peter 2:4.

But left their proper dwelling. “Proper dwelling” (oikētērion) is home, habitation: heaven. They walked out of the presence of God. Their position did not protect them; it made their fall greater.

He has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day. A wordplay: they did not keep (tērēsantas) their position, so God keeps (tetērēken) them in chains. The contrast with verse 1 is sharp: believers are kept for Jesus Christ; these angels are kept for judgement. Everyone is kept by God for something. “Eternal chains” (desmois aidiois). “Great day”: the final judgement. The contrast between their former dignity and their present condition is total: from the presence of God to eternal chains in gloomy darkness. Authority and status are not shields against accountability. They are responsibilities that increase it.

Who are these angels? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning; many Jewish and early Christian readers, and many today, link them with the sons of God of Genesis 6:2, and Jude’s next words, likewise about the sexual sin of Sodom, support that link. Calvin and many Reformed writers read Genesis 6 as the line of Seth instead. The more likely reading is the Genesis 6 one, but the point stands either way: God judges rebellion.

If these angels are in chains, why are demons still active? Jude speaks of a particular group confined until the judgement, not of all fallen angels; others are still at work under God’s restraint (Ephesians 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8).

Just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities. The third example. The surrounding cities were Admah and Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23), the cities of the plain.

Which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire. “Likewise”: like the angels, they crossed boundaries God set. “Indulged in sexual immorality” (ekporneusasai) is gave themselves over to immorality. “Unnatural desire” (sarkos heteras) is literally other flesh, different flesh. The men of Sodom sought sexual relations with the visitors (Genesis 19:4–5), who were angels, and their sin included same-sex intercourse. The phrase may emphasise both: pursuing flesh of a different kind (angels, unknowingly), and desire contrary to God’s design.

What was the sin of Sodom? Ezekiel names pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49), and Genesis shows the men of the city demanding sex with Lot’s visitors (Genesis 19:5). Jude adds that they indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire. The visitors were angels, but the men of Sodom took them for men; their desire was against the created order, and Jude names it as sexual sin. The passage confirms the rest of Scripture that same-sex sexual practice is sin, among the other sins of a proud and godless city.

Serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire. “Example” (deigma) is a sample, a specimen, a display. The cities of the plain did not merely face judgement; they became an exhibit, a permanent warning sign in the landscape of sacred history. Sodom had Abraham’s nephew Lot living in its midst, a righteous man (2 Peter 2:7), and Abraham pleading for it before God. “Eternal fire” (pyros aiōniou). The fire that destroyed the cities is a picture of the eternal fire of final judgement (Matthew 25:41). The fire on the plain of Jordan was a sample. The real fire is still coming.

Where Christians differ: is punishment eternal, or do the wicked cease to exist? Annihilationists hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist; universalists that all are eventually saved. Verdict: Jude speaks of eternal chains and eternal fire (vv. 6–7) and utter darkness reserved forever (v. 13). Jesus used the same word, eternal, for both punishment and life (Matthew 25:46). Scripture teaches conscious, eternal punishment for those who reject God (Revelation 14:11; 20:10). This truth is held with sorrow and with urgency to warn and to rescue (v. 23).

How can a loving God punish for ever? Because sin is not a small offence against a small god, but rebellion against the infinitely holy and good Creator, and because those who persist in rejecting him go on rejecting him. Hell is God giving people, justly, what they chose: life without him, which is darkness. We must not soften what Jesus himself taught more than anyone. But the same God who will judge has done the most costly thing imaginable to rescue us: he sent his Son to bear the fire in our place. The doctrine of hell is not a reason to doubt his love but a measure of it, and a summons to run to Christ and to warn others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean those who struggle with same-sex attraction are beyond grace. All sinners may be washed and forgiven (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). It means sexual immorality of every kind is serious before God.

I experience same-sex attraction, or love someone who does. What does this mean for us? It means you are not a special category of sinner; every believer battles disordered desires, and temptation itself is not sin. The call is the same for all Christians: to deny ourselves, take up the cross, and follow Christ in holiness, which for every unmarried believer means chastity. The church must be a place where such believers are welcomed, loved, befriended and supported, not shamed or isolated. And for anyone who has fallen, the word of 1 Corinthians 6:11 stands: such were some of you, but you were washed. Christ receives all who come.

In a sentence. Though you already know all this, I want to remind you that Jesus, who delivered his people out of Egypt, later destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not keep their positions of authority but abandoned their proper dwelling, he has kept in darkness, bound with everlasting chains for judgement on the great Day. In a similar way, Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding towns gave themselves up to sexual immorality and perversion. They serve as an example of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire.

On a Tuesday. Do not trust your history: your baptism, your upbringing, your church role. Trust Christ today, and keep trusting him. And pray for those still under judgement, by name. If someone you know assumes that being religious or having once made a decision means they are safe while living in open sin, find a gentle moment to ask them where their trust really is.

For worship. Jesus brought his people out of Egypt with a mighty hand. He opened the sea, fed them with bread from heaven, and gave them water from the rock that was himself. He is holy, and those who refused to trust him fell in the wilderness. Angels fell, and cities burned. And yet the same Jesus came down to bear judgement for those who believe, so that the fire that will fall on the ungodly fell first on him. We are rescued from the judgement we deserved, not because we were better than Israel or Sodom, but because our Saviour is merciful and mighty, and he has never lost one whom he truly brought out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The False Teachers: A Portrait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude now paints the false teachers in image after image: they defile, reject authority and mock what they do not understand; they walk the road of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are reefs, clouds without rain, dead trees, foaming waves and wandering stars. Each image describes people who promise nourishment and give nothing, or worse.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Portrait of False Teachers

Even Michael would not pronounce judgement on the devil but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” These men blaspheme what they do not understand, and walk in the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They shared the church’s love feasts while feeding only themselves.

Now: Beware teaching that looks impressive and spiritual but leaves people no closer to Christ and no more holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.

Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams. “Relying on their dreams” (enypniazomenoi) is dreaming: claiming visions and revelations as authority for their teaching and conduct. False prophecy based on dreams was an old problem (Jeremiah 23:25–32), where the prophets said I have dreamed, I have dreamed, and God answered that they prophesied the deceit of their own heart. This is the first detail about the false teachers’ self-understanding. They put private experience above the faith delivered. It is the ancient form of an appeal that has never gone away: God told me directly, offered as justification for setting aside what God has revealed publicly and permanently. The appeal to private revelation as a licence for moral departure from the apostolic faith is not a modern invention; Jude was already dealing with it in the first generation.

Defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. Three charges, matching the three examples: immorality (Sodom), rebellion against authority (Israel, and the angels who left their position), and contempt for spiritual beings. “Glorious ones” (doxas) are angelic beings, as in 2 Peter 2:10. The false teachers are re-enacting the old patterns all at once.

The glorious ones. The glorious ones are most likely angelic beings, as in the parallel at 2 Peter 2:10–11; the false teachers mocked spiritual powers they did not understand. Michael’s restraint (v. 9) shows the right attitude.

But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses. The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it comes from a Jewish tradition, perhaps recorded in a lost work called the Assumption of Moses. God buried Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5–6), and the tradition said the devil claimed his body. Michael is the archangel, the great prince who protects God’s people (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1; Revelation 12:7). Jude chooses the most powerful of the holy angels to give the most devastating comparison available.

He did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment. Instead he said, “The Lord rebuke you.” Michael, mighty as he was, left judgement to God (compare Zechariah 3:2, where the angel of the LORD says the same to Satan accusing Joshua the high priest). He did not insult Satan in his own authority. He did not say I condemn you, or be gone, you rebel. The judgement belongs to God, and even the archangel will not take it into his own hands. Now set that beside the false teachers, who speak with contemptuous confidence about things beyond their knowledge. Michael, with far more authority and understanding than these teachers, showed far more restraint. The comparison is not subtle. It is meant to expose their presumption as the absurdity it is.

Should Christians rebuke the devil, then? Even the archangel did not pronounce judgement on him in his own authority, but left it to God: “The Lord rebuke you.” Believers are to resist the devil by faith, God’s word and prayer (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11–18), not to mock him, address him with bravado or claim authority to bind him. The battle is the Lord’s.

But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand. Arrogance born of ignorance. The less they know, the more freely they speak.

And they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. What they do understand, their animal instincts and appetites, is what destroys them (2 Peter 2:12). The irony is complete: they claim a higher knowledge of spiritual things, and the only knowledge they really have is the knowledge of a beast, which leads where a beast’s appetite always leads.

Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain. One woe and three examples: Cain, Balaam and Korah. The woe is not a curse word; it is prophetic judicial language, the same woe Jesus pronounced on the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23). Cain represents envy, hatred, murder, and rejecting God’s way of approach (Genesis 4; 1 John 3:12). He brought an offering of his own choosing, was angry when it was not accepted, and killed his brother whose offering was. It is religious self-will turning into hatred of the righteous.

And abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error. Balaam represents greed, the prostitution of a genuine spiritual gift for money, leading God’s people into immorality and idolatry for a fee (Numbers 22–25; 31:16; 2 Peter 2:15). “Abandoned themselves” is literally poured themselves out, rushed headlong: not a slip but a plunge.

And perished in Korah’s rebellion. Korah represents rebellion against God’s appointed leaders, Moses and Aaron, for which the earth opened and swallowed him (Numbers 16). “Perished” is past tense: their fate is as good as sealed. Three Old Testament cases, three patterns of spiritual failure: hatred, greed, and pride. The false teachers are walking in all three.

These are hidden reefs at your love feasts. Five vivid pictures from nature follow. “Hidden reefs” (spilades) are rocks hidden below the water, on which ships are wrecked; the word can also mean stains, spots. “Love feasts” (agapais) were the fellowship meals of the early church, often with the Lord’s Supper. The false teachers were present, hidden dangers. A reef looks like calm water until the hull tears open.

As they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves. “Without fear” (aphobōs) is without reverence, at the very table where Christ’s death was remembered. They eat the community’s food and share its fellowship while destroying it from within. Shepherds feeding themselves is the precise inversion of the pastoral calling (Ezekiel 34:2, 8): shepherds exist to feed the flock, not to feed from it. These are leaders who care only for themselves.

Waterless clouds, swept along by winds. Clouds that promise rain but give none (Proverbs 25:14, where a man who boasts of a gift he does not give is like clouds and wind without rain). In a dry land, clouds on the horizon meant hope; waterless clouds are deception made visible.

Fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted. Trees that should be bearing fruit at harvest but have none (Matthew 7:17–19). Autumn is when fruit should be there, and it is not. “Twice dead”: dead in fruitlessness and dead with roots torn up; perhaps spiritually dead and destined for the second death (Revelation 20:14). “Uprooted”: their end is complete removal. Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up (Matthew 15:13).

Wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame. Restless, raging, leaving filthy foam and debris on the beach (Isaiah 57:20, where the wicked are like the tossing sea, whose waters toss up mire and dirt). All turbulent energy, no nourishment, only refuse at the shore. A great deal of noise and movement, and what it leaves behind is shame.

Wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever. “Wandering stars” (asteres planētai) are planets, or shooting stars, or perhaps fallen angels in Jewish imagery. It is the most haunting image. Sailors navigated by the fixed stars; a star that wanders is unreliable for navigation and leads sailors astray. The teacher who cannot be trusted to hold the apostolic faith does not merely fail to guide; he actively misleads those trying to find the way. Their destiny is eternal darkness. Those who would not shine with a steady light will lose all light.

Five pictures, one diagnosis. Look at the five images together and they cover every realm of nature: sea, sky, earth, sea again, heavens. Wherever you look, these men are failures of promise: a reef that looks like calm water, a cloud that looks like rain, a tree that looks like harvest, a wave that looks like power, a star that looks like a guide. Each one appears to offer something and delivers nothing, or worse than nothing. That is what false teaching is.

Textual note. Jude draws on Jewish traditions that are not in the Old Testament, here and in verses 14–15. Quoting or alluding to a writing does not make that writing Scripture; Paul quoted pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Jude’s inspired use affirms the truth of the particular point he cites.

Someone tells me God gave them a dream or a word for me. How should I respond? Kindly, but with Scripture in hand. This app holds that new revelatory gifts ceased with the apostles, though we hold that view charitably toward brothers who differ. Either way, no dream or word may contradict Scripture, add to the faith once delivered, or override plain obedience. If what is said agrees with the Bible, you need the Bible, not the dream, to know it is true. If it disagrees, set it aside, however sincere the person. And be especially wary of any claimed revelation that excuses sin, demands money, or puts a leader beyond question; that is exactly what Jude describes.

How can I tell whether a church leader is feeding the flock or himself? Watch what he does with Scripture, people, money and correction. A true shepherd opens the word faithfully and points to Christ, not himself. He knows and cares for ordinary members, especially the weak and the troubled. He is open about money and does not live off the flock lavishly. He welcomes accountability and can be corrected. A self-feeding shepherd is the reverse: his sermons centre on himself, he courts the influential, he is evasive about finances, and he punishes those who question him. Where a leader abuses people, it must be brought into the light and the victims protected; Christ’s sheep are not his to use.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should fear demons or be preoccupied with angels. It means they should not be arrogant about spiritual matters, and should leave judgement to God.

In a sentence. In the very same way, on the strength of their dreams these ungodly people pollute their own bodies, reject authority and heap abuse on celestial beings. But even the archangel Michael, when he was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not himself dare to condemn him for slander but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” Yet these people slander whatever they do not understand, and the very things they do understand by instinct, as irrational animals do, will destroy them. Woe to them! They have taken the way of Cain; they have rushed for profit into Balaam’s error; they have been destroyed in Korah’s rebellion. These people are hidden reefs at your love feasts, eating with you without the slightest qualm, shepherds who feed only themselves. They are clouds without rain, blown along by the wind; autumn trees, without fruit and uprooted, twice dead. They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved for ever.

On a Tuesday. Test teachers by their fruit: are they serving the flock or themselves? Are they giving water or just promising it? Then turn the test on yourself. In the places where you lead, at home, at work, in a small group, are you feeding others or feeding yourself? Is there any of Cain’s envy, Balaam’s love of gain, or Korah’s resentment of authority in you? Name it before God today.

For worship. Against every image of failure stands Christ. He is the rock on which no one is wrecked, the cloud that pours down rain, the true vine whose branches bear fruit, the Lord who stills the wild waves with a word, and the bright morning star who never wanders. He is the Good Shepherd who does not feed on the sheep but feeds them, and lays down his life for them. Cain killed his brother; Christ died for his brothers. Balaam sold his gift; Christ gave himself freely. Korah grasped at authority; Christ, who had all authority, took the form of a servant. Where false shepherds fail, he never fails, and his flock is safe.
verseByVerse.note: The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it was known from Jewish tradition. Cain, Balaam and Korah stand for murderous hatred, greed and rebellion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude quotes a prophecy found in 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read in his day: the Lord is coming with countless holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words. He says Enoch “prophesied”; he does not say the book is Scripture. Its message matches the rest of the Bible (Daniel 7:10; Matthew 25:31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prophecy of Enoch

Jude cites a true prophecy from 1 Enoch without calling the book Scripture: the Lord will come with his holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers grumbled, boasted and flattered people for gain.

Now: A true shepherd says what people need to hear; a false one says what pays.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.' These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.’ These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.

It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied. Enoch walked with God and was taken (Genesis 5:18–24; Hebrews 11:5), one of only two people in Scripture of whom it is said that they did not die; Elijah is the other. “Seventh from Adam” counts Adam as the first: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch. The designation also appears in 1 Enoch itself, and it marks Enoch’s closeness to the beginning: before the flood, before Abraham, before Moses, this man was already warning of the Lord’s coming. Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time (1 Enoch 1:9), perhaps the most widely read Jewish apocalyptic text of the period. Jude does not call 1 Enoch Scripture, but affirms that this particular prophecy is true, perhaps preserved by tradition from Enoch himself.

Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones. “Comes” (ēlthen) is literally came, a prophetic past: as certain as if already done. “Ten thousands” (myriasin) is myriads, a number meant to suggest an uncountable multitude. “Holy ones” are angels (Deuteronomy 33:2; Zechariah 14:5; Matthew 25:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7). The imagery of the Lord coming with a vast heavenly retinue runs through the Old Testament (Daniel 7:10) and into the New (Revelation 19:14). The sheer number communicates the overwhelming, irresistible nature of the coming judgement. When that day comes, the false teachers’ bluster will be entirely silent.

To execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly. “Convict” (elenxai) is a legal word: to expose, to prove guilty conclusively before a court. This is not an emotional accusation but a judicial finding. The ungodly will not merely be condemned; they will be shown to be condemned, their guilt made undeniable even to themselves. And the word all is repeated, and ungodly appears four times in one sentence: their whole character is ungodliness. The judgement is comprehensive in scope, all people and all deeds, and exact in its target. Nothing is overlooked; nothing that was hidden will remain hidden.

And of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him. “Harsh things” (sklērōn) are hard, defiant words. God judges words as well as deeds (Matthew 12:36–37). Every careless sneer at God, every mocking word against his Christ, is heard and recorded.

These are grumblers, malcontents. Verses 15–16 close the portrait by describing the false teachers in their daily behaviour. “Grumblers” (gongystai) are murmurers, like Israel in the wilderness, who grumbled against Moses and against God (1 Corinthians 10:10). The word sounds like what it describes, a low discontented muttering. “Malcontents” (mempsimoiroi) are complainers about their lot, blamers of fate: people who always find something wrong with what God has given them.

Following their own sinful desires. Ruled by desire. Their complaints and their lusts are connected: a heart that will not be content with God’s provision goes looking for its own.

They are loud-mouthed boasters. “Loud-mouthed” (hyperonka) is swelling, bombastic, as in 2 Peter 2:18. Big words, little substance.

Showing favoritism to gain advantage. “Showing favouritism” (thaumazontes prosōpa) is literally admiring faces: flattering. They flatter the influential for profit (James 2:1–9). The detail about flattery is especially revealing. These teachers cultivated relationships of apparent admiration in order to extract what they wanted. They said what their audience wanted to hear, and their audience rewarded them for it. It is the oldest and most seductive form of false ministry: telling people what they want to hear, gaining influence, and using that influence for personal benefit. And notice the combination: boastful toward God and flattering toward men. Grumbling about God, they fawn over people who can pay.

Where Christians differ: does quoting 1 Enoch make it Scripture? The Ethiopian Orthodox Church includes 1 Enoch in its canon. Verdict: Jude quotes one prophecy from 1 Enoch and affirms it as true, as Paul quoted true statements from pagan poets. This does not make the whole book inspired. The church, including Jesus and the apostles, did not recognise 1 Enoch as part of the Hebrew Scriptures, and it contains much that is legendary. The canon is closed and does not include it.

Is 1 Enoch Scripture, then? Jude quotes a prophecy found in the book of 1 Enoch and says that Enoch truly prophesied this. Some think Jude regarded the book as inspired. The more likely reading is that Jude affirms this particular prophecy as true, as Paul quotes true lines from pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), without endorsing the whole book, which neither the Jews nor the church received as Scripture. A true statement is true regardless of where it is found, and the Holy Spirit led Jude to use this one.

Is grumbling really that serious? Scripture treats it as far more serious than we do. Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness was counted as unbelief and rebellion against God (Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). Grumbling says that God has given me less than I deserve and that he is not managing my life well. It poisons fellowship, spreads quickly, and is often the first sign of a heart drifting from God. The remedy is not pretending everything is fine, since the psalms are full of honest lament brought to God, but thankfulness and contentment (Philippians 2:14; 4:11–13). Lament takes the pain to God; grumbling talks about God behind his back.

How do I tell flattery from genuine encouragement? Encouragement tells the truth in love for the other person’s good; flattery tells pleasing untruths for the flatterer’s good. Encouragement is specific and honest and will also, when needed, include correction (Proverbs 27:6). Flattery is vague and excessive, is aimed especially at those with power or money, and never risks a hard word. If someone only ever tells you what you want to hear, be careful. And when you encourage others, give thanks for real evidences of grace in them, and be just as ready to say a difficult word gently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grumbling is a minor sin. Scripture treats it as rebellion against God’s providence.

In a sentence. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about them: ‘See, the Lord is coming with thousands upon thousands of his holy ones to judge everyone, and to convict all of them of all the ungodly acts they have committed in their ungodliness, and of all the defiant words ungodly sinners have spoken against him.’ These people are grumblers and faultfinders; they follow their own evil desires; they boast about themselves and flatter others for their own advantage.

On a Tuesday. Watch for grumbling in your own heart this week. Replace it with thanks. Each time you catch yourself complaining, about the weather, the boss, the church, your circumstances, stop and name one specific gift of God instead. And speak no word to anyone this week that you would not want to hear again on the day the Lord comes with his holy ones.

For worship. From the seventh generation of the world, a man who walked with God was already announcing the coming of the Lord, and the Lord is coming still. He comes with myriads of his holy ones, not to be judged but to judge, and every word spoken against him will fall silent before his face. And yet this same Lord, before he comes in glory, came in humility: the Judge stood in the dock, was convicted in our place, and bore the sentence. So the day that will expose the ungodly holds no terror for those who are hidden in him. Enoch walked with God and was taken. We walk with God through Christ, and one day we too will be taken into his presence, to go no more out.
verseByVerse.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time. Quoting it does not make it Scripture; Paul also quoted pagan poets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — Hold Fast: The Call to the Faithful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “But you, beloved.” Jude turns from the false teachers to the people he loves. The apostles foretold such scoffers, so their arrival is no reason to panic. Then he gives the faithful their task: build yourselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, wait for Christ’s mercy, and rescue those in danger, each in the way they need.
verseByVerse.theology:
But You, Beloved

Build yourselves up in the faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, and wait for Christ’s mercy. Then show mercy to the wavering and snatch others from the fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles had foretold scoffers in the last time.

Now: Meet each person where they are: patience for the doubting, urgency for the endangered, and care for yourself in the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.' It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, ‘In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.’ It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.

But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. The sudden turn in address marks the letter’s pivot. For several verses the false teachers have been held up in the light, their corruption exposed. Now Jude speaks directly to the people he loves. Beloved: this is who they are to him, whatever the crisis. The pastoral relationship survives the alarm. “Remember” (mnēsthēte). “Predictions” (rhēmatōn) are words spoken beforehand. The apostles warned of this. Paul told the Ephesian elders that after his departure fierce wolves would come in among them, not sparing the flock (Acts 20:29–30). He told Timothy that in later times some would depart from the faith (1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1–5). Peter warned of scoffers who would deny the Lord’s return (2 Peter 3:3). Jude seems to speak of the apostles as a past generation. And this matters pastorally: the person who knows that false teaching was promised is less likely to be disoriented when it arrives. The map includes the difficulty. We are not lost.

They said to you. “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.” “Last time” is the whole period since Christ’s coming. “Scoffers” (empaiktai) are mockers, as in 2 Peter 3:3. The apostolic description of the false teachers matches Jude’s. Their theology serves their lifestyle. They have not reached their conclusions by honest inquiry and found that the conclusions happen to free them from moral restraint; they have decided what they want to do and then constructed a theology to justify it. This is the basic pattern of antinomian theology in every generation: the ethics come first, and the doctrine follows to legitimise them.

It is these who cause divisions. “Cause divisions” (apodiorizontes) is make separations, draw boundaries. Perhaps they claimed to be a spiritual elite, dividing the church into first- and second-class Christians: those who had the dreams and the higher knowledge, and the ordinary believers who did not.

Worldly people. “Worldly” (psychikoi) is natural, soulish, unspiritual, as in 1 Corinthians 2:14 and James 3:15: living at the level of unregenerate human nature, by natural human nature and not by the Spirit. Ironic, if they claimed superior spirituality.

Devoid of the Spirit. “Devoid of the Spirit” (pneuma mē echontes) is literally not having the Spirit. This is the decisive mark: they are not Christians at all (Romans 8:9). It is the most devastating thing Jude can say about them, and he says it last in the portrait. All their claims to special spiritual experience, all their appeals to dreams and visions, and they do not have the Spirit. The one thing they most loudly claim to possess is the one thing they most conspicuously lack. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). The fruit of the false teachers is division, licentiousness, grumbling and self-promotion. The tree is known by its fruit.

How do I know whether I have the Spirit? Every true believer has the Spirit; there is no second class of Christians who lack him (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). The evidence is not dramatic experiences but the Spirit’s ordinary work: you confess Jesus as Lord from the heart (1 Corinthians 12:3); you cry to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16); you love Christ and his word; you fight sin and want holiness; you love other believers; and his fruit is growing in you, however slowly. If you see these, however faintly, the Spirit is at work. If you do not, ask God for his Spirit, for he gives the Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Is every division in the church caused by people like this? No. Some separations are necessary, when the gospel itself is denied (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10). And many divisions among true believers come from ordinary sin, misunderstanding or honest disagreement on secondary matters, as between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). What marks Jude’s divisive people is that they split the church around themselves, claiming higher spirituality, while living for the flesh. Before you separate from other believers, ask whether the issue is the gospel or your preference, and whether you have truly sought peace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every division in the church is caused by unbelievers. But those who divide the church by claiming a higher spirituality while living for the flesh show they lack the Spirit.

In a sentence. But, dear friends, remember what the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ foretold. They said to you, ‘In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow their own ungodly desires.’ These are the people who divide you, who follow mere natural instincts and do not have the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of a church split, a celebrity pastor’s fall or a new false teaching, do not be shaken: the apostles said it would happen. Then ask whether you contribute to division anywhere: by gossip, by a party spirit, by looking down on other believers as less spiritual. Seek out one fellow Christian this week whom you have been inclined to dismiss, and treat them as a brother or sister.

For worship. The Spirit whom the scoffers lack has been given to every one of God’s children. He is the pledge of our inheritance, the seal of our belonging, the One who cries Abba, Father, in our hearts. He does not divide the body of Christ into the elite and the ordinary; he baptises all into one body and gives each a share. And Christ, who sent him, warned us beforehand through his apostles, so that when the wolves come we will not be surprised, but will know that our Shepherd saw them first and has not left us without his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.

But you, beloved. “But you”: in contrast with the scoffers. Now Jude gives the positive instructions. Verses 20–21 cluster three participles around one central command, keep yourselves in the love of God. The grammar is important: the keeping is the command; the three activities are the means.

Building yourselves up in your most holy faith. “Building up” (epoikodomountes) is building on a foundation. It is not a passive reception of instruction but an active construction, a deliberate building of the life of the church on the foundation of the apostolic faith. “Most holy faith” is the apostolic faith (v. 3), holy because it comes from God. The superlative of holiness is applied not to a behaviour but to a body of belief. The faith itself is sacred; it is set apart, it is the Lord’s. Build your life on it, growing in knowledge of Scripture and sound doctrine (Colossians 2:7; Acts 20:32). And notice the plural: yourselves. This is done together, as a church.

And praying in the Holy Spirit. “Praying in the Holy Spirit” (en pneumati hagiō proseuchomenoi) is prayer guided, empowered and inspired by the Spirit, according to God’s will (Romans 8:26–27; Ephesians 6:18). It is not merely human effort but Spirit-enabled communion with God; the Spirit intercedes for us, and prayer in the Spirit means coming into line with his own intercession. The Spirit whom the scoffers lack (v. 19) helps believers pray.

Where Christians differ: does “praying in the Holy Spirit” mean praying in tongues? Some charismatic believers take it as speaking in tongues. Verdict: Nothing in the context mentions tongues. Praying in the Spirit means praying under the Spirit’s guidance and in dependence on him, according to God’s will revealed in his word (Ephesians 6:18). All believers can and should pray this way.

Does praying in the Holy Spirit mean praying in tongues? Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read it so. But Paul uses similar words of all prayer, praying at all times in the Spirit (Ephesians 6:18), and nothing here mentions tongues. The more likely reading is prayer led and helped by the Spirit and in line with his will.

Keep yourselves in the love of God. The main command. “Keep” (tērēsate) is guard, preserve, echoing verse 1 (kept for Jesus Christ) and verse 6 (the angels who did not keep their position). God keeps them; they keep themselves in his love. Remain where God’s love can be enjoyed, by obedience and fellowship: abide in my love, Jesus said, and if you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love (John 15:9–10). Jude does not say make God love you; that is already settled (v. 1). He says stay in the place where that love is known and enjoyed, as a man stays by the fire on a cold night.

If God keeps us, why are we told to keep ourselves in the love of God? Both are true (vv. 1, 24). God keeps his people, and he does it through their keeping themselves: building up their faith, praying and waiting for Christ’s mercy. Our effort is the means of his keeping, not a rival to it (Philippians 2:12–13). That is why Jude can end with full confidence in him who is able to keep you from stumbling.

Waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. “Waiting” (prosdechomenoi) is eagerly expecting. “Mercy” is the mercy Christ will show at his return, bringing believers into the fullness of eternal life. The horizon of the Christian life is not the end of this age but the mercy of Christ at his appearing. The mercy here is the same mercy Jude opened with in verse 2. They have received mercy; they are waiting for more of it, its final and fullest form, when Christ comes. Even at the judgement, what believers look for is not reward for merit but mercy. Note the Trinity: Holy Spirit, God the Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ, all in two verses.

And have mercy on those who doubt. Then the rescue mission of verses 22–23, the most finely judged pastoral instruction in the letter. Three groups need different responses. “Those who doubt” (diakrinomenous) are those who waver, who are unsettled: believers shaken by the false teachers. These are not the committed false teachers but people whose faith has been disturbed and who are genuinely uncertain. They need compassion, not condemnation. Show them patient, compassionate help.

Save others by snatching them out of the fire. “Snatching” (harpazontes) is seizing, grabbing quickly. Those already deeply influenced, on the edge of destruction, need urgent rescue. It is the language of emergency, as if someone were already inside a burning building; it recalls the brand plucked from the burning (Amos 4:11; Zechariah 3:2). There is no time for lengthy discussion; they must be pulled out.

To others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh. Those most deeply corrupted. Still show mercy, but with caution, with fear, lest you be dragged down too (Galatians 6:1). “Garment stained” (spilōmenon chitōna) is a soiled undergarment: an image of moral pollution (Zechariah 3:3–4, where Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments and God takes them away and clothes him in pure ones). The image is of a rescuer who must enter a contaminated place: the rescue is not cancelled, but the rescuer must be careful not to be contaminated in the process. Love the sinner, hate the sin, and beware its contamination.

One approach does not fit all. This threefold pattern is one of the most practically wise pieces of pastoral instruction in the New Testament. The same approach does not work for everyone. The person gently wavering needs gentle mercy. The person rapidly falling needs urgent intervention. The person deeply entangled in the false system needs a rescuer who is both merciful and on guard. To learn these distinctions is to love people as they actually are, rather than forcing everyone through a single formula.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ in verses 22–23, some describing two groups, others three. The ESV follows the three-group reading, which has good early support.

A friend is doubting. What do I actually do? Start with mercy, as Jude says. Listen properly before you answer; find out what the doubt really is, whether intellectual, moral or born of suffering. Do not be shocked or impatient. Share your own struggles where it helps. Point to Christ himself more than to arguments: read a Gospel together, or a psalm of lament. Offer a good book if the question is intellectual, but stay with them; doubt is often lonely. Pray for them and with them. Keep them in the fellowship of the church. And be patient: many doubters come through to a stronger faith.

How do I help someone caught in sin without being pulled in myself? Go humbly, aware that you could fall too (Galatians 6:1). Do not go alone when the sin is one that tempts you; take a mature believer. Set clear boundaries: do not linger in the places or conversations where the sin lives. Keep your own walk with God close through prayer, Scripture and accountability. Speak clearly about the sin and warmly about Christ. If the person is unrepentant and the sin serious, involve the church’s elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Mercy is the goal; fear is the guard.

What it does not mean. Keep yourselves does not mean salvation depends on our own power to keep ourselves. God keeps us (vv. 1, 24); we actively keep ourselves by the means he provides.

In a sentence. But you, dear friends, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you to eternal life. Be merciful to those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; to others show mercy, mixed with fear, hating even the clothing stained by corrupted flesh.

On a Tuesday. Is someone you know wavering in their faith? Reach out to them with mercy this week. Then check the three means of keeping in your own life. Building: are you feeding on God’s word and sound teaching? Praying: are you praying in dependence on the Spirit, not just in emergencies? Waiting: are you looking forward to Christ’s mercy at his coming? Pick the weakest of the three and give it attention today.

For worship. The love of God is a fire on a cold night, and he invites us to stay close to it. He gives us the most holy faith to build on, the Holy Spirit to help us pray, and the mercy of Christ to wait for. And he sends us, in his mercy, to others: to the doubting with patience, to the endangered with urgency, to the defiled with careful love. That is his own way with us. He was patient when we doubted, he snatched us from the fire, and he took off our filthy garments and clothed us in his own righteousness. Every rescue we attempt is a small echo of the great rescue he has done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter that began with alarm ends in adoration. After so many examples of those who stumbled, Jude lifts our eyes to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless with great joy. The doxology is not an add-on. It is the ground on which the whole letter stands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Him Who Is Able

The letter full of stumbling ends with the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless before his glory with great joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church under pressure was pointed to God’s glory, majesty, dominion and authority.

Now: The same God holds his people through every crisis, and will bring them home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.

Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling. “Able” (dynamenō) is has the power. The opening phrase of the doxology is not a rhetorical flourish but a declaration. God is not merely willing to keep his people; he is able. In a letter about the danger of falling, about those who did fall, Israel, the angels, Sodom, this is the answer that reframes everything. “Keep” (phylaxai) is guard, protect, as a sentry guards. “From stumbling” (aptaistous) is without falling, sure-footed, like a horse that does not stumble; the word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The letter begins with believers kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1) and ends with God able to keep. Perseverance rests on God. The stumbling you fear, the ground you might lose, the false teaching that might overwhelm you: the One who keeps you is the One who spoke creation into being and holds it together by the word of his power. He is not a safety net at the bottom of the cliff; he is a shepherd on the path, keeping the feet of his sheep.

And to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy. “Present” (stēsai) is cause to stand: the language of formal presentation before a king or a court. The ones being kept are not merely admitted to the presence of glory; they are made to stand there. “Blameless” (amōmous) is without blemish, the word used of a sacrifice without defect, the animal that could be offered to God because it was without spot (Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22). Every believer who has felt the weight of their own failure should hear this word. They will be presented spotless, not because they were in themselves without fault, but because the One who keeps them also cleanses them, and the One who presents them guarantees the presentation. “His glory” is God’s glorious presence. “Great joy” (agalliasis) is exultation, leaping joy, the kind that breaks out of ordinary expression: God’s joy and ours, as the bride is presented to the bridegroom. It is the joy of the father running to meet his returning son (Luke 15:20), of the shepherd laying the lost sheep on his shoulders (Luke 15:5), the joy set before Christ for which he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2). The homecoming of the saints is a joy to God.

Will I really be blameless? I know how much I still sin. Yes, and not because you will one day manage it yourself. Christ gave himself up for his church to present her to himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). His blood has already cleansed you of guilt, and at his coming he will complete your sanctification: you will be like him, for you will see him as he is (1 John 3:2). There is no purgatory to pass through; the finished work of Christ is enough. Your present sin should make you humble and watchful, but not hopeless. The One who began a good work in you is the One who will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).
